archetype.name: Rebuilding (run-stopping, pass-leaking)
archetype.definition: A first-year staff running a patient, efficient offense in front of a pass defense that still can't cover anyone, which is essentially the same team that went 3-14 last year.

report.headline: Same leaky secondary, new coach: a middling offense can't outscore it.
report.take:
Mike LaFleur inherited a team that finished 26th in net EPA last season. Four games in, the Cardinals sit 27th. The record is honest. A 1-3 mark with a 30-point deficit projects to about 1.3 wins, and the turnover margin is slightly positive. Arizona isn't unlucky. It is a below-average team whose one win came against a Chargers offense now ranked 31st.

The split between the two units explains everything. The offense is functional: 11th in success rate, 6th in run success and 6th in time of possession. Jacoby Brissett gets the ball out in about 2.6 seconds, which keeps the sack rate 8th-best. The problem is that it produces almost no big plays. The pass offense is 23rd in EPA, and the targets run through Trey McBride (46) and Michael Wilson (44), while Marvin Harrison Jr. has only 13 in four games. When the short game works, Arizona hangs around, as in the 30-36 loss at San Francisco. When it doesn't, the passing game collapses: -8.1 pass EPA on 95 yards against Seattle and -18.2 with three turnovers against the Giants.

The defense is two different units. Against the run it is 5th in EPA allowed and 7th in missed-tackle rate, so the front tackles well. Against the pass it is 31st, 31st in explosive pass rate, 30th on deep balls and 31st on short throws. That is a coverage problem at every depth, and a 20th-ranked pressure rate isn't hiding it. It also isn't new: this defense ranked 26th by EPA last year and 31st in 2023. Owning the clock (31.9 minutes a game) and still allowing 29.3 points tells you how efficiently opponents move when they do have the ball.

The outlook got worse this week. Left tackle Paris Johnson Jr., a 100%-snap starter, is out for the season, and guard Isaiah Adams is questionable. A quick-throwing offense can hide some of that, but not all of it, and the schedule still includes two games each against the Rams and Seattle, plus Kansas City and Las Vegas.

strengths.title: A front that stops the run
strengths.body: Arizona is 5th in rush EPA allowed and 7th in missed-tackle rate, so opponents aren't breaking runs through tackles. This looks structural rather than fluky, since it holds across all four games by EPA. The cost is that it pushes opponents toward throwing, which is exactly where this defense breaks.

strengths.title: Efficient, clock-controlling offense
strengths.body: An offense ranked 11th in success rate and 6th in run success sustains drives and wins the possession battle (6th in time of possession). It rests on staying on schedule rather than on explosive plays. That makes it repeatable, but it limits how much it can score.

strengths.title: Quick release limits sacks
strengths.body: Brissett's 2.6-second average release is among the quickest in the league. It is a big reason the sack rate is 8th and the QB-hit rate 7th. That protection is partly scheme and partly the line, and the line just lost its 100%-snap left tackle, so expect some slippage.

concerns.title: Pass defense broken at every depth
concerns.body: Arizona is 31st in pass EPA allowed, 31st on short throws, 30th on deep throws and 31st in explosive pass rate. With pressure only 20th, this is a coverage problem, not just a rush problem. History says it's chronic, with the defense ranked 26th last year and 31st in 2023, and the safety group is thinned with Wingard questionable and Taylor-Demerson out.

concerns.title: Left tackle lost for the year
concerns.body: Johnson played every snap before a biceps injury ended his season, and guard Adams (81% of snaps) is also questionable with an ankle injury. The quick-game offense will protect the backups somewhat, but an offense that already lacks big plays can't afford more drive-killing negative plays.

concerns.title: Passing game has no middle gear
concerns.body: Pass EPA has swung from +9 and +10.1 to -8.1 and -18.2. The Giants loss brought three turnovers, and Seattle held the team to 95 passing yards. Without vertical threats (Harrison Jr. has 13 targets), a stalled short game has nothing to fall back on. That is a structural flaw rather than variance.

trend.note: The opening win came at the Chargers, whose offense ranks 31st. The defense then allowed 31, 36 and 36 points. The offense alternated between good and broken weeks, ending with a three-turnover loss as a favorite in New York.

nextGame.headline: Shootout setup: Goff's passing attack meets the NFL's leakiest secondary.
nextGame.body:
Detroit is the worst possible stylistic draw for this defense. The Lions pass offense is 4th in EPA, and Arizona's run defense, its one strength, matters less against a team that ranks 17th running the ball and likes to throw. The good news is on the other side: Detroit's defense is 32nd in EPA allowed, 32nd on third down and 31st in the red zone. That suits an Arizona offense built on sustaining drives. The danger is the Lions' 15 sacks, 2nd in the league, against a line missing its left tackle.

Availability cuts both ways. Arizona loses Johnson for the year, has Adams, Love (55 carries) and safety Wingard questionable, and has Taylor-Demerson out at safety. Detroit is also banged up: guard Bartch (93% of snaps) is out, center Mays is on IR, corner Ya-Sin is expected to sit, safety Harper is on IR and Branch is still working back. A thinned Lions secondary is the opening Brissett's short game needs.

keyMatchups.title: Goff's pass game vs Arizona coverage
keyMatchups.body: Detroit is 4th in pass EPA. Arizona is 31st in pass EPA allowed and 31st in explosive passes allowed. Unless the 20th-ranked Cardinals pass rush gets home, this is where the game tilts.

keyMatchups.title: Lions rush vs patched-up left side
keyMatchups.body: Detroit has 15 sacks and ranks 6th in sack rate. Arizona's quick release has kept its sack rate low, but now it does so without Johnson and possibly without Adams. Negative plays are what turned the Seattle and Giants games.

keyMatchups.title: Ball control vs a soft third-down defense
keyMatchups.body: Arizona's best path is long drives that keep Goff on the sideline. Detroit allows conversions on 52.8% of third downs (32nd) and touchdowns on 82.4% of red-zone trips (31st), so the Cardinals should finish drives at a better rate than usual.

restOfSeason.body:
Little here points to regression in either direction. The point differential matches the record and the turnover margin is mildly positive, so there's no luck to give back or bad luck to recover. The pass defense has been bad for most of the past four seasons and should stay bottom-five. The offense's efficiency is real but low-ceiling, and losing Johnson trims it further.

The schedule offers winnable games against Washington, Philadelphia (29th-ranked offense), the Jets, the Saints and Denver, plus a Dallas defense ranked 31st. It also includes two Rams games and a Seattle game against top-four defenses, Kansas City, Las Vegas and San Francisco's top offense. Picking off three to five of the softer games is a realistic ceiling for a team at this level.
swingFactors: Whether the line holds up without Johnson

bets.reason: Both defenses are bottom-five by EPA allowed (Detroit 32nd, Arizona 28th), and Detroit's games have averaged 61.6 combined points. Arizona's last two games hit 66 and 60. The risk is Arizona's clock control shortening the game, which is why this is a lean and not a like.

Detroit is 0-4 against the spread and only 18th in net EPA, about 0.045 per play ahead of Arizona. That gap plus Arizona's home field argues for a line closer to a field goal. The Johnson injury against the league's 2nd-ranked sack defense keeps this small.

confidence.note: Four games, a first-year staff, and the left tackle just lost for the year.
